AN AWMIA, lhpisro DKM-M.D. On Monday. at Warrington Police court, a young fellow named Ilarrop Chadwick was summoned on a charge of having oven on liCenAell premises during prohibited hours, on the Ist inst. From a state- ment made by the I hief Constable it appeared that at about 5.31 on the morning in question defendant went moth., 11,1 den Lion Inn, Knutsford-rowl, and knocked loudly at the door. John Williamson, the landlord, was awakened, and defendant asked him for some whisky for his wife, who was very ill. lie had, he soil, come by the direction of a doctor. lie alto made the same representation to a police- man, and was ultimately supplied with a pint of whisky, for which he pail two shillings. At shout tista), however, defendant returned and asked for another pint of whisky. and the landlord, having I become suspicious, declined to serve him and in. a seNeant of police of what had occurred. It was afterwards found that the story about a doctor having Femt him for whisky was a fabrica- tion. A tine of 10s. anti costs' or 14 days' imprison- ment in default, was imposed.

As ACTIII.WB Marion Ashton, an actress, whose theatrical name is" Dolly Marshall," Wit 4 again before Warrington borough court, y...der lay. Oh aoh irg-t it using malicious threats to Isabella Daley. another actress. Mr. A. Browne pros,euted on behalf of complain- ant, and from his statement it appeared that Miss Daley had been engaged at the Theatre Royal, War- rington, during the last two or three weeks. During the whole of that time she hail beenannoyed, in the theatre, outside the theatre, and in the streets by the defendant, who called her filthy names. On Tuesday night she got into the theatre dressed as a factory girl, and while the complainant was on the stage, she shouted from the auditorium, Look at : that filthy prostitute." It wa." also stated that defendant had threatened to kill that— before I ain done with her." Several witnesses were called on behalf of the complainant. Defendant denied: point blank that she had said or done any of the things alleged against her. and she remarked that she would "not put herself in jeopardy for ouch a creatunt." and added that it was very strange if she could not go into Scotland-road because some- body else was living with her husband." She was bound over in her own recognisances of £lO to keep the peace for six months.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON RANGERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON RANGERS.

The first match of this annual fixture took place at Broughton on Saturday afternoon, when a good atten- dance assembled to witness the proceedinp. Valor. ' tunately, Warrington were not able to place their full strength in the field for no important a contest, no less than five of the playersoriginally selected to &duty crying off, and when ito taken into account that those players were Lawless, Antrobus, and Speakman from the back division, and Frank Turner and Jolley from the for- wards, the very fact of Warringt in making a draw, to all intents a moral victory, speaks volumes of praise for those players who officiated in their stead. Although Saturday's match was not of a first class description, there were at timrebrilliancy and neatness in the War- ringtonians' play that made the most biassed spectators cheer, but the visitors certainly experienced hard luck on more than one occasion, a glaring instance of this being witnessed in the effort between Barnes and Massey is the second half, when the last-named grounded on the wrong ride of the line The Rangers too had au atrienter, Battersby, whohaS now figured twice against the War- ringtonians, namely, in the St. lit-tens anti Swinton en- counters. The ground was in a wretched condition. Fare Turner kicked off against a slight tweete. The oval travelled at a rapid pace all over the field, until its destination was found at centre. Here play was chiefly confined, the bulk eef the work falling to the lot of the forwards. Both sides acquitted themselves with credit, and Squires made an effort, only to find a stumbling block in Barnes. Evans received a neat pass from Bate, anti a strong run found play once more at neutral ground. Samson, who it may be mentioned officiated at full back in the second team, was called upon to defend, and his kick travelling to Rope, this : prominent player gave the visiting side a taste of his abilities by running and kicking, taking the oval to the Warrington quarters. The wirepuller+ " retaliated, and with the aid of Bate and Lawless play was again contested at half way flag. Free kicks were freely indulged in, neither side claiming an advantage, until a movement by Massey, Bate, and Barnes found Warring- ton in an aggressive attitude. Neat Passing by the Warrington backs looked like scoring, until Gresty interrupted and transferred the leather to Midfield. Handles got away from a line-out, but still no impres- sion could be made, for a good rush by the home front van Rent the leather to Barnes, wh with tricky work brought the ball out and punted well into touch at the quarter flag. Passing by LAM.A. Bate, Barnes, and Evans was neutralises' by Hoyle. and Samson in daring fashion pureed the ball out, and luckily cleared his linen. Grady hero mulled a pass, but Skidmore taking advan- tage rushed the oval to the visitingemarter flag,Evans ftc a run through the thick transferring hostilities to the home twenty-five. A penalty kick was met by Nevins who returned' in true style and Rnyle touched down Another goad movement by the visiting threr-quarters was well taken up by their forwards, and Hoyle was again compelled to save, this latter iton bringing about half-time, the score reading as follows ,—Warrirpton, 0-0-2, Broughton Rangers, nil. Motion resumes', and judicious kriteria by Barnes and Massey caused the Rangers to adopt defensive tactics. Bate showed up with a pretty run from a line-out, and it looked as if Inc was going to repeat his performance of twelve enenths one until a timely push by McGowan stay's' his career. Alters series of exeltanges by the opposing barks, tante smart pressing by Bate, Barnes, anil Massey caused Hoyle some uneasiness, but another brilliant pass to Massey found the speedy Warrington three-quart, making for the line, unfortunately grounding on the wrong side. Boyle and Samson then exchanged with advantage to the Rangers' custodian, anti a smart run and kick by thirsty was instrun ~ ~ tal in taking the play to the Warrington end. Play was destined to stay here but momentarily, for a fine rude of the visiting forwards, chief amongst whom were Nevins, Ashton, Povey, and 1101011, took the leather over, but for some informality the point mac din. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. By OLYMPIAN.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. By OLYMPIAN.
FI.TBALL-RVOTIY,

To-dity's match.o i—Warringtnn v. Kondal Hornets a t Warrington ; Runcorn V. Burton-on-Trent at Burton ; Widnes v. Crompton at Crompton ; St. Helens v. Stipa at Aspull ; St. Helens Rees. v. Stockport at Stock- port.

Warrington were rather weakly represented on Saturday but they undoubtedly had the upper hand of Broughton Rangers. Nevins, a sterling forward who has not been seen much of lately, a.gain donned the jersey on behalf of Warrington, and did some gaol work. With so many absentees the combination of the •• wirepullers " was bound to be somewhat broken, but thry otiS pressed the Broughtonians so severely at times that it woo hard lines for them a divisive point was not scored. The homesters were fortunate in having their crack man, Boyle, at full back, for he saved them from disaster more than

The Yorkshire v. Middlesex match was looked forward to for a fine exposition of the Rugby game, but it turned ; out to be something of a disappointment. Yorkshir4 ! seems to be decidedly on the down grade this season. She in beginning to find that it is easy enough to get rid of the Sutcliffe, and Loekwoods, but not no easy to fill their places.

Runcorn very unexpectedly found in New Brighton on Saturday almost the toughostnut they havehad to crack this season The lirightonians played with admirable dash and combination and until the second half was well under way they bad the verdict in points. Runcorn were determined, however, not to have their record spoiled, and, after showing some of their best qualities, ran out winners—but only by a neck, no to speak. Ropes were entertained ill Runcorn that the fine play of their centre, Crompton, would meet with recognition by his selection to do duty in the match North v. South, but there has been disappointment. But Crompton can afford to wait. Re is young yet, and if he keep up his past form there is little doubt that he will be sought after some of these days.

The St. Helens RON. got an unexpected beating their own ground, last Saturday. and for "o bit of a change" they had the uncongenial experience of being nilled.” And this, too, by their friend:4 the Tyldes- leyita!

After the somewhat erratic performanee. of the Den- ton's Green Club against Tyldesley, the Heca: supporters were jubilantly confident as to what they would do when they had the opportunity. But what a fall ! Their cup of expectation was doomed to crush in pieces at their feet: and whatever the Rees. playsrs accoinplished, this is what Tyldeslay did Tyldesley 1-0.7, Recreation 0-0-0.

The match between St. Helens and Levenshulme was a " runaway' affair for the Foreman brigade. Levens- hulme arrived short-handed, and got the assistance of two subs, but they were unable to stem the onward rushes of the honmsters, with whom victory rested by the big margin of two goals, four tries, and four minors, ton blank sheet.

div.head: FOOTBALL-AELSOCTATION.
div.p: FOOTBALL-AELSOCTATION.

Local Associationist organisations appear to have had a holiday last Saturday. St. Helens sustained a six to none ch:feat at the feet of Stanley ; Earlestown were " galloped mod" by the Higher Walton lads to the tune of 10 jrrials to none ; and Hardock—Wl4l. Haydock, perhaps wisely, had a genuine holiday and were without a fixture.

The remnants of the St. Selena A.F.C.' to the total of 9 men, all told, including the umpire, who was premed into service, did wvll against their agile and powerful Opponents, and showed a gond defensive game. Instead , of six goals being scored against them it would not have occasioned much surprise if there had been 16. -- CRICKET.

The list of cricket fiXiti-res-i--I:r the season of 1890 arranged by the county secretaries is published. In addition to the engagements of the first-elms counties, , the matches in the second class are given, as well as the fixtures for the Universities and the Australian team. It ! was also decided on Tuesday by representatives of the eight first-class counties, that in future drawn games should be set aside in deciding the county champion- ship.

Twelve persons wen- crushed to death. and seventy-five others injured, many fatally. Several ladies are miming. The building, wf,iiml i.n small,was crowded, the audience • being composed fif the most part of women and children. div.head: SHOCKING BURNING ACCIDENTS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SHOCKING BURNING ACCIDENTS AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday night two patients were admitted to the Warrington Infirmary, each suffering from , severe burns. Margaret Ilansbury a girl of Rix ' years, whose parents live in Naylor-at., was fort ; shalt time left in the bowie by herself. Sho was ' warming her hands at the fire; her clothing became ignited, and she was burned about the face, arms, and chest. The other patient, Drift:et Kelly, 49 years of age, WCYIVeR her injuries at her home, en Oliver-at. She was standing 011 the fender in order to reach some- thing, when her clothing caught fire, and she also was severely horned. She rushed out Ras the street with Iher garments in flames and several neighbours promptly rendered assistance. . . s

On Sunday the younger patient. HausburiNsuommhed to her injuries, and on Tuesday morning NIT W. T. Hun- hand, deputy-coroner, held an inquest in the Parade- room, at the Police Stmion, touching the death. It appeared from the evidence that the deceased was alone in the house on Saturday evening, when she went to the I tire, as she subsequently told her father at the Infirmary. to warm her hands, an she felt cold. Iler pinafore caught fire, and she ran intothe street. Patrick Shaugh- nessy, labourer, Naylor-an, said he saw the child in the street, and her clothes were in flames. He took off his cant, wrapped it round her, and put out the flames. The child was taken to the Infirmary, where she died on the following day.—lnspector spins : Wittiess's hands were slightly burnt—The Coroner I think he acted very bravely.—Tbe jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: RACK 10 BACK BOUTUL
div.p: RACK 10 BACK BOUTUL

Back-to-back houses make another serious evil which is very prevalent in the North-East ward, though by no means confined to that ward. It is needless to say that houses such as those, without any through ventilation, are everywhere condemned as seriously defective from a sanitary point of view. flosses of this sort, like unpaved yards, are to he found in probably all the older parts of the North- East ward, and it is pretty often seen that the back-to-back house has an unpaved and sloppy yard, a broken down closet, and on unflagged pas. age. The residents in these houses 'move. AS a rule a very practical knowledge of the weak sole of, Corporate administration in Warrington. It is not necessary to enumerate the locality of all the houses of this description. but, some good samples of them may be found in the courts and yards off Dial-st., RIO Fennell-st., at Silver-nt.. and Old Gardens, off Ilaydock-st., and on Town Hill.

div.head: , THE FARNWORTH ELOPEMENT CASE.
div.p: , THE FARNWORTH ELOPEMENT CASE.

In the Divorce Division, on Wednesday, before Mr. Julia' Britt, an application was made in reference to the ease of Bush v. Bush and Anderson, osrently reported, I in which a jury asses:eft dainag. at £4,000. The I petitioner wag a solicitor, of Bath and Trowbridge, and he obtained a decree nisi for the dissolution of his mar- riage on the ground of his wife's adultry with the co- respondent, who was described as a gentleman of means who had resided near Liverponl. Argo:ding to the evi- dence at the trial the crerespondent had eloped with Mrs. Bush, after paying his arldreana to her sorter, to whom lie was engaged. Mr. Searle, or behalf of the petitioner, stated that his lordship had directed that the damages should be recovered by the petitioner, and then paid into court. It had been ascertained that the co- respondent became entitled to one-third of the sum of £lO,OOO left by his grandfather, and the nfnney Was in the hands of his trustees. The application wits for an order that the money be paid forthw'th instead of in a fortnight. Mr. Searle alns asked for the appointment of a receiver.—llis Lordship pointed out that he could not alter the order behind the hack of tl e en-respondent. . and he could not appoint a receiver. He had no moat to suppose that the co-respondent would not pay—Mr. Searle said tire difficulty was that they did not know where the co-respondent was.—His Is : In my , opinion, thereis no ground for these applications, and I . must refuse thorn.

div.head: EXECUTION OF k WIFE MURDERER.
div.p: EXECUTION OF k WIFE MURDERER.

Benjamin Purnell was executed on Monday morning at Ilerises Gaol, for the murder of his wife at Devizes on November 9th. Purnell and his wife lived uncomfort- ably together, and he killed her with a hatcher during a quarrel. The culprit , who has exhibited little remorse, walked firnily to the scaffold, and death was instantane- nos. Three executions have taken place at Devizes since the passing of the Prirate Executions Acts, .nn, arid all the culprita have belonged to Bradford-on-

div.head: CIIESIIIRK COUNTY POLICE.
div.p: CIIESIIIRK COUNTY POLICE.

Sir—An the Chief Constable has not thought fit to reply to toy letter regarding police irregularities, I have brought the whole of the case before the notice of the Home Secretary. A well-known Member of Parliament will also bring the matter before the House of Cmnmons when Parlia- ment meets. Meantime it will be interesting to notice what action will be taken by the, Standing. Joint Com- mittee. Unless the Clunmitree is to be a standing sham and a fares. it will never permit such a state of affairs as I hmnve pointed out to exist another day.—Yours faithfully, SLATE' Stecbfonl, Binningham, 12 DK. 1889.
J. SLATER LEWIS.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL, AND THE
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL, AND THE
VAN lIEN.

bir,—Mr. Alderman Burgess is reported:to have said, at Town Council meeting, on Tuesday, in reference to tht deputation from the Warrington Traci. Council, on the question of the dinner hour to the ash cart and van men, that so far as the committee knew the matter did not originate with the men themselves;; and the men had no eomplaint to make. Now, sir, I have to say that the ' matter did originate with the men themselves ; a I continuous complaint was made by the men ; or the Trades Council would not have interfered where there was no complaint. The deputation told the rommittee, at their Mat interview, that the men wiahed them to Witercede on their behalf, and that they did so at the earn- est requeat of the men, thus showing that the Trades Council had no motive of their own in taking the matter up.—Yours he.
W. BULLOCK, All:retnry. 10, Brackley-et., Warrinron, De, sth, 1889. -
ALLEGED BOYCOTIING AT RUNCORN.

Sir.—Having had much evidence in the past of your desire to open your columns for the ventilation of any grievance, I avail myself of the provost opportunity of acquainting you with an extraordinary case of •• boy- cotting which came under my notice, and which, if true, needs some strong disapprobation on the part of the Runcorn public generally. It is as follows Mr. Thompson, the phrenologist, is, *5 000 are aware, giving popular lectures on mental science, M the Public Hall; and my curiosity being aroused I attended and found a poor and meagre attendance, which was explained by the lecturer, in :1 few warm caustic sentences, as being the result of a " boycott " ordered to be set up by the Runcorn Musical Society for his refusal to let them have the hall for their concert on the 17th inst. Now, if this is correct, it shows that we hove in our midst a public body who can resort to contemptible expedients to bring about the discredit of any opponent wlm stands in the way of the furtherance of their ends. I deeply regret, .4 citizen of Runcorn, such doubtful means to success, and desire to express, through you, my strongest dis- approbation in which I trust to have 3:our sympathy and support. Thanking you in anticipation foe the insertion of this letter.—l am, yours km,
THEM v. ERROR.

My letters have evidently touched his conscience, but perhaps he may be one of those individual named by Paul, " under a strong delusion to believe lies " ; not much of a brother to writo such rubbish. As U. his allusion to my " dostroying Popery with sealona reckless- sess:' he omits to tell no it is the Popery inside the Church of England as practised by the English Church Union, aided by such men as Bishops of Lincoln and Smithwell, the latter only recently wearing a picture of , the Virgin Mary and child on his back, the former orowned ; whilst at Ely they have issued a look an : Mariolatry. The proof of Ritualism (alias Romanisrn is to be Ewen in Warrington through a Reformssl Church being built there, and on Wednesday there is to be a meeting of churchmen at Chester Town Hall with a similar object. div.p: THE SHIP CINAL.
T.NQI:FST AT BARTON.

IMr. PG, held at impiest on Wednesday at the Ship Canal Hospital, Barton, on the body of George White. ! hind, 32, who resides in IVarburtim-st., Salford. j Deceased mono labourer on the Ship Canal works, and I on Monday morning, the 2nd inst., was working in a I rotting or trench near Pomona Gardens. The dirt and I rock got out of the cutting were hoisted to the surface in a skip by means of a strain crane. As the skip was full, I and was about to be hoisted, another workman named I Merin Janney placed three workmen's picks on the top of it. The handles of the picks projected over the side of the skip, and when near the top of the cutting one of them caught a plank and fell into ths trench, striking the deceased on the head. He was taken to the hospital at Barton, and died on Monday last. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and the Coroner severely reasoned Janney for placing the picks no earelessly oath..
